analysis.one_liner: Sends $20 billion to states to protect nursing home residents from COVID-19.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 9 cosponsors during the pandemic, the bill was referred to committee on May 22, 2020 and never received a markup or floor vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have sent $20 billion to states and tribal governments to help nursing homes, intermediate care facilities, and psychiatric hospitals separate residents by COVID-19 status — a practice called cohorting — so infected residents could not spread the virus to healthy ones. The money could pay for testing kits, protective equipment, extra staffing, hazard pay for workers, and converting hotels or dormitories into temporary care facilities. It also would have required monthly Health Department briefings to Congress and protected residents from being discharged for failure to pay.
analysis.who_benefits: Older adults and people with disabilities living in nursing homes, intermediate care facilities, and psychiatric hospitals, who were at extreme risk from COVID-19 outbreaks in shared rooms and hallways. Direct care workers would benefit from premium pay, sick leave, childcare, and housing support funded by the bill. States, tribes, and residents unable to pay for their own care would also receive support.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Nursing home residents and care workers

how_it_helps.text: Appropriates $20 billion for fiscal year 2020 for payments to states and Indian Tribes to support separating residents based on COVID-19 status in skilled nursing facilities, nursing facilities, intermediate care facilities, and psychiatric hospitals.

Funds may be used for testing kits, personal protective equipment, additional staffing including surge teams, premium or hazard pay, paid sick and family leave, and retrofitting hotels, dormitories, schools, and churches as temporary care facilities.

Requires the Health and Human Services Secretary to issue guidance on which facilities may cohort, with eligibility accounting for a facility's compliance history on infection control and its record under the special focus facility program for chronically underperforming homes.

Includes consumer protections: facilities may not discharge residents for failure to pay, and residents and their families must get written notice at least 72 hours before a discharge or transfer, with ombudsman contact information.
Requires monthly briefings to congressional committees on the outbreak in these facilities and an Inspector General report evaluating the Secretary's response.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through a $20 billion appropriation from the Treasury not offset by other spending. Nursing homes would also face conditions: guidance ties funding eligibility to a facility's infection-control compliance record.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers; underperforming facilities face scrutiny

drawbacks.text: The $20 billion is appropriated 'out of any monies in the Treasury not otherwise appropriated' with no offset, adding to federal spending during a period of emergency deficit-financed relief.

Participation runs through state applications and voluntary facility compliance rather than federal mandates, so facilities that declined to cohort could simply forgo the funds and continue pre-pandemic practices.
The money flows to the existing nursing home industry rather than building new capacity, reinforcing facilities whose compliance records the bill itself flags as a risk factor.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — protecting a population that suffered some of the worst COVID-19 death rates, in close-quarters settings where one infected resident could infect many — was large and time-sensitive; every week of delay in May 2020 mattered. The costs are real but modest by comparison: $20 billion in emergency spending and dependence on state administration. The main design weakness is that participation was voluntary for facilities and contingent on state applications, which could have left the worst homes untouched precisely where the risk was highest.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on May 22, 2020 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which never took it up; it died there when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Anna Eshoo introduced the bill on May 22, 2020, joined by original cosponsors including Reps. Schakowsky, Shalala, Dean, and Moulton.
Nine House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did.

The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on the day of introduction and saw no further action — no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — in the remainder of the Congress.
Because the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 without enactment, the bill expired and would have needed to be reintroduced from scratch.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nursing home operators avoided $20 billion in funding that would have come conditioned on cohorting residents and tied to their infection-control compliance records, and taxpayers avoided the $20 billion appropriation. The cost fell on nursing home and psychiatric facility residents, who got no dedicated federal cohorting program from this bill during the pandemic.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nursing home operators; residents gained nothing

for.name: Anna Eshoo
for.role: U.S. Representative (D-CA); Chair, Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it as sponsor.

against.name: Frank Pallone
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referred bill and never scheduled it for a committee markup or vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All ten supporters in the record — the sponsor and nine cosponsors — were House Democrats, but the bill never reached a vote, so Republicans never took a recorded position on it.

industries.industry: Nursing homes and long-term care facilities
industries.note: The bill routes $20 billion through these facilities for testing, protective equipment, extra staffing, and hazard pay — money the facilities and their workers would receive. Its interest runs alongside residents' here, though the bill ties eligibility to each facility's infection-control and special-focus compliance record, directing scrutiny toward chronic underperformers.

industries.industry: Direct care workers (aides, nurses, pharmacists in congregate care)
industries.note: The bill funds premium and hazard pay, overtime, paid sick and family leave, childcare, temporary housing, and transportation for facility staff, who faced high infection risk working with COVID-positive residents.

industries.industry: Hotels, dormitories, and other non-traditional property owners
industries.note: States could use funds to retrofit hotels, dormitories, schools, and churches as temporary care facilities, creating paid conversions. Any gain depends on states choosing this option.
The bill designates these Medicare-contracted organizations to provide technical assistance to facilities on infection control and staffing, a paid role under the program.
